AFTER 6.30PM MASS, AFTER DAILY MASS (UNLESS THERE’S A FUNERAL), OR ON REQUEST. “In all four Gospels Pilate asked Jesus, “Are you the king of the Jews?” Many of you will know the Church of Christ the King in Cabra which is dedicated to today’s feast day. It was opened in October 1933 by Archbishop Byrne. Outside the church, there is a striking statue of Christ the King which was sculpted in Trieste. It’s a very grand statue which I am sure has made a strong impression on parishioners over the years. This morning we celebrate the Feast of Christ the King which is the last Sunday in our Liturgical Year. This feast was instituted on its current date as a Solemnity by Blessed Paul VI in 1969. Next week is the First Sunday of Advent, the beginning of the new church year. In our Gospel today, we are presented with the parable that we have come to know as the sheep and the goats. It appears at the end of Matthew’s gospel and also near the end of the life of Jesus, when he was confronted with the scribes and pharisees. The possibility of salvation, of keeping the inheritance of the reign of God, depends on the practice of justice and mercy for those who suffer from different needs. Jesus says in Chapter 18 of St John’s Gospel: “Yes, I am a king. I was born for this, I came into the world for this: to bear witness to the truth; and a ll who are on the side of truth listen to my voice.” In all four Gospels Pilate asked Jesus, “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus is indeed a King is this story but, from a human point of view, is a very unusual King. He rules from the cross and his gifts to us are forgiveness, mercy, and eternal life. The crown that Christ wears is a crown of thorns. The kind of Kingship that Jesus is talking about is very different to what we might regard as a brash regal figure with great powers ruling over a large territory. In fact, it is the complete opposite. Jesus’s power of love can be seen in the way he forgives, shows mercy and is open to everyone. In Luke 17:21 " Jesus tells us that” the kingdom of God is among you". So, as we come to the end this Church year let us reflect on the presence of Jesus in our lives, what direction they are taking and how we can become more in tune with what Jesus may be asking of us as we approach the Season of Advent. St Paul tells us in Chapter 12 of the Letter to the Corinthians to “Be ambitious for the higher gifts”. In other words, as Church or as Christian people, we should not always settle for the status quo but be prepared to look for new ways to share the Gospel message with our parishes and our communities. It’s a good challenge for us all as we celebrate the Feast of Christ the King. We should also remember today the words of Pope Francis who reminds us that “God, in his l oving design, excludes no one.” That is an important message of hope as we celebrate the Feast of Christ the King.
